848.title: Mata Sundari's letters
848.hook: her hukamnamas guided the scattered sangats in these years
848.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Mata Sundari as a guiding presence for the Khalsa after Guru Gobind Singh, and hukamnamas, letters of instruction, are still issued from the Akal Takht and read aloud in gurdwaras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two slips of paper in the Amritsar pool, and two Khalsas who agreed how to decide before they knew the answer. Your line was settle it fairly. Did you get to propose a fair way? Day eight hundred forty-eight.

A rider arrives at a village after days on the road. He carries a folded letter. The sangat, the local gathering of Sikhs, comes together to hear it read aloud. Someone opens it carefully. It begins with a blessing. It names them. It tells them to keep the Guru's way, to stay together, to send what help they can. Then it's folded again and kept. There was no Guru in a human body anymore. The Khalsa was scattered and hunted. And from Delhi, a widow was writing letters. Today: Mata Sundari's letters.
screen: `A RIDER WITH A FOLDED LETTER.` → `THE SANGAT GATHERS TO HEAR IT.` → `A WIDOW IN DELHI, WRITING.`

segments.voice: Mata Sundari was the wife of Guru Gobind Singh. After the Guru passed, Sikhs believe the Guruship rested in the scripture and the Khalsa together, so no one would sit on the Guru's seat again. But people still needed someone to hear their questions, to steady them, to say keep going. Tradition says that role fell, in large part, to her. She lived in Delhi, and from there she wrote hukamnamas. A hukamnama is a letter of instruction, an order given with authority and love at the same time. The Gurus had written them before her. Now the letters went out in her name to sangats in villages and towns far away. What did they say? Tradition remembers them asking sangats to keep to the Guru's teachings, to gather and sing, to support the community's work, and to stay united when they were pulled apart. Some tellings say she also took practical steps, sending Bhai Mani Singh to Amritsar to care for the Harmandir. So yesterday's story and today's are tied together: the man at the pool was there, tradition says, because she sent him. Here is what's striking. She held no army. She held no throne. She had ink, paper, riders and a name that people trusted. In a time when gathering openly could cost a life, a letter could reach a place a crowd could not. A sangat holding her hukamnama knew someone far away was thinking of them by name. Then the letter was folded again, and kept.
screen: `THE GURU'S WIFE, IN DELHI.` · `A HUKAMNAMA: A LETTER OF ORDER.` · `KEEP THE WAY. STAY TOGETHER.` · `SHE SENT BHAI MANI SINGH.` · then, large: `INK, PAPER, AND A TRUSTED NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: encourage someone far away. Settle, and let the breath be easy. Bring to mind one person who is at a distance from you, in miles or in years. Someone going through something hard. Picture them where they are right now. Then let a few plain words form, the kind you would put in a letter. Their name first. Then one thing that is true and steadying. Don't polish it. Just let it be honest. If you pray, you can hold them in mind and say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Mata Sundari's letters. The hukamnamas Guru Gobind Singh's widow sent from Delhi to scattered sangats, telling them to keep the way and stay together. Today's word.
Your line: letters in hard times. Today, send one real message to someone far away, using their name, with one true and steadying thing in it. Day eight hundred forty-eight.

849.title: Living in the forests
849.hook: with a price on their heads, Sikhs lived on horseback in forests and deserts
849.howItsDone: Sikhs tell stories of the forest years in gurdwaras and at home, and remember them in the daily Ardas, which honors those who held to the faith through persecution.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Sundari's letters, read aloud to sangats far from Delhi. Your line was letters in hard times. Who did you write to? Today, the people those letters were trying to reach. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

A saddle for a pillow. A blanket that is also a cloak. A cooking pot tied behind, and the reins never far from your hand, even asleep. Tradition says that in these years whole Sikh families had no address at all. The governors in Lahore had put a price on a Sikh's head. A village that sheltered them could be punished. So the Khalsa moved into the places nobody wanted to follow: thick forests along the rivers, the dry country to the south, the edges of the desert. Today: living in the forests.
screen: `A SADDLE FOR A PILLOW.` → `A PRICE ON THEIR HEADS.` → `INTO THE FORESTS AND DESERTS.`

segments.voice: What did that life look like? The tradition remembers bands of horsemen, called jathas, moving from one hiding place to the next, never staying long. They ate what they could find or what friendly villagers slipped them in the dark. They slept in shifts. When soldiers came close, they scattered and met again somewhere agreed in advance. A horse was not a possession. It was the house, the escape, the way to bring food home. And here's the surprising part. Out of that hard life came humor. The Khalsa developed its own way of speaking, sometimes called Khalsa bole, the Khalsa's words, and some of it is a joke against hardship. Some tellings say a handful of dry chickpeas was called almonds. A lone rider might call himself an army. It sounds like bravado, and maybe it was. But it was also a way of refusing to let the hunt decide how they felt. It's the chardi kala this path met in the hills after Lohgarh, turned into a joke. The Gurus' hymns were with them too. Riders who knew them by heart could recite the morning and evening prayers in a forest clearing as easily as in a town. A gurdwara needs walls. The Name, the tradition says, does not. Where the riders stopped, the sangat was. Some readers hear one more thing in these stories: a reminder that a roof, a bed and a door that locks are not ordinary at all.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be grateful for your roof. Sit where you are and let the breath settle. Then notice what is above you. A ceiling. A roof. Walls on every side. A door. Feel the floor holding you up, dry and level. Let your attention move slowly through the room: the light, the warmth or the cool, a place to sleep tonight. Don't rush past any of it. Just let each one register as a gift. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for each thing you notice. The bell holds the time.
Living in the forests. The years when the hunted Khalsa had no fixed home, and lived on horseback in forests and deserts, with the Name and a joke for company. Today's word.
Your line: home was a horse. Today, when you walk through your own door, stop for one breath and say thank you for the roof. Day eight hundred forty-nine.

850.title: Bota Singh and Garja Singh
850.hook: tradition says two Sikhs set up a toll on the highway to prove the Khalsa was still alive
850.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Bota Singh and Garja Singh as a picture of chardi kala, high spirits under persecution, and it is often retold in gurdwara talks and children's classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living in the forests, a saddle for a pillow. Your line was home was a horse. Did you stop at your own door and say thank you? Day eight hundred fifty.

Two travelers pass a clump of bushes by the road. They glimpse a man hiding there, and one says to the other, loud enough to be heard: that can't be a Sikh. The Sikhs are finished. And if any were left, they wouldn't hide. Tradition says the man in the bushes was Bota Singh. And that sentence stung him more than any sword. Today, a quiet story with a loud ending: Bota Singh and Garja Singh.
screen: `A MAN HIDING BY THE ROAD.` → `THE SIKHS ARE FINISHED.` → `THEY WOULDN'T HIDE.`

segments.voice: In the hunted years, tradition says, the governor's men claimed the Khalsa had been wiped out. Bota Singh had been living rough, slipping into Amritsar at night to bathe in the sacred pool and then disappearing again. When he heard the travelers, he decided the claim needed an answer. So he and his companion Garja Singh walked out of hiding and did something almost absurd. They picked a spot on the great highway near Tarn Taran, by a roadside inn, armed themselves with heavy clubs, and set up a toll. Every cart paid a small coin. Every donkey, a smaller one. And, tradition says, they collected it. Travelers paid. Nobody quite knew what to do with two Sikhs standing calmly in the middle of the road as if they owned it. Then Bota Singh did the boldest thing of all. He wrote a letter to the governor in Lahore, telling him who was collecting tolls on the king's highway. A message that said, in effect: still here. Soldiers were sent. The two did not run. Tradition says they fought until they fell. Now, notice what they were not doing. They were not stealing for themselves. They were not trying to win a war two men could not win. They were making a point that only their presence could make: the Khalsa is alive. The travelers had said a Sikh would not hide. Bota Singh and Garja Singh decided that, this once, they would not. Two clubs, a few coins, and a letter with a name on it.
screen: `THE KHALSA IS FINISHED, THEY SAID.` · `A TOLL ON THE GREAT HIGHWAY.` · `A LETTER TO THE GOVERNOR.` · `THEY DID NOT RUN.` · then, large: `STILL HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: show up when it counts. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind one place where your presence would say something. A friend's hard day. A meeting you've been skipping. A family table you've been avoiding. A cause you care about but have only watched. Picture yourself walking in and simply being there. Not giving a speech. Not fixing everything. Just present, so no one can say you weren't. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bota Singh and Garja Singh. The two Sikhs who, tradition says, set up a toll on the highway and wrote to the governor to prove the Khalsa was still alive. Today's word.
screen: `BOTA SINGH AND GARJA SINGH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: still here. Today, show up in person for one thing that matters, and stay long enough to be counted. Day eight hundred fifty.

851.title: The Diwali permit, 1734
851.hook: Bhai Mani Singh arranged a Diwali gathering at Amritsar, was unable to pay the tax, and was executed
851.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Mani Singh at Diwali and in the daily Ardas, which recalls those who were cut limb from limb rather than give up their faith; Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj in Lahore marks the place tradition gives for his death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bota Singh and Garja Singh, standing on the highway with a toll and a letter. Your line was still here. Where did you show up? Today, the man from the pool returns. Day eight hundred fifty-one.

Diwali at Amritsar. Lamps on the water, the Harmandir glowing, Sikhs coming in from every direction to bathe, to listen, to see each other's faces. In the hunted years, that gathering had become impossible. So a man who had served the Guru himself went to the governor in Lahore and asked, formally, for a permit. He was Bhai Mani Singh, the same Sikh who, tradition says, had once settled the quarrel of the two slips in the pool. The governor named a price. Bhai Mani Singh agreed to pay it. Today: the Diwali permit.
screen: `LAMPS ON THE WATER.` → `BHAI MANI SINGH ASKS FOR A PERMIT.` → `THE GOVERNOR NAMES A PRICE.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the plan was simple. Sikhs would come for Diwali, offerings would be made, and from those offerings Bhai Mani Singh would pay the fee he had promised. But word reached him that the governor meant to use the gathering as a trap, to send soldiers among the crowds. So Bhai Mani Singh did the one thing that would ruin his own position. He sent messages telling the Sikhs not to come. Think about the cost of that choice. He saved the people. And he guaranteed that the money would not be there. Few came. The offerings fell short. He could not pay. He was arrested and taken to Lahore. There, tradition says, he was offered his life if he would give up his faith. He refused. And the sentence was terrible: to be cut apart, joint by joint. Sikhs remember those who died this way. In the Ardas, the standing prayer said at the close of Sikh services, the sangat recalls those who were cut limb from limb and did not give up their faith, and tradition places Bhai Mani Singh among them. He was not only a martyr. Tradition remembers him as a scholar and scribe, a man who had served Guru Gobind Singh closely and who cared for the Harmandir for years. A whole life of careful, patient service ended in one refusal. The permit was a piece of paper. What he kept was not on paper.
screen: `A FEE FOR A DIWALI GATHERING.` · `A TRAP: HE TELLS SIKHS NOT TO COME.` · `HE CANNOT PAY.` · `OFFERED HIS LIFE. HE REFUSES.` · then, large: `HE KEPT FAITH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one sacred promise. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one promise you've made that matters to you. To a person, to God if you pray, to yourself. Maybe it's been slipping. Maybe it's been costing more than you expected. Don't judge it. Just hold it in front of you, and feel its weight. Then choose one small way to keep it today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The Diwali permit. The fee Bhai Mani Singh promised for a Diwali gathering at Amritsar; when he warned Sikhs away and could not pay, he gave his life rather than his faith. Today's word.
Your line: he kept faith. Today, keep one promise that matters to you, even if keeping it costs you something. Day eight hundred fifty-one.

852.title: Nawab Kapur Singh
852.hook: offered a Mughal title, the Khalsa gave it to a man who was fanning the sangat, and he accepted humbly
852.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Nawab Kapur Singh as a lesson in seva, and gurdwara volunteers still serve the sangat in small ways, including fanning, sweeping and cleaning shoes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Diwali permit, and Bhai Mani Singh, who warned the Sikhs away and paid with his life. Your line was he kept faith. Which promise did you keep? Day eight hundred fifty-two.

A hot day. The sangat sits together at Amritsar, and the air barely moves. At the edge of the gathering, one man stands with a large hand fan, slowly moving the air over everyone else. Nobody asked him to. It's his seva, his service. Meanwhile a messenger has arrived from Lahore with an astonishing offer from the governor: an estate, a robe of honor, and the title of Nawab, a lord. The Khalsa has to decide who, if anyone, will wear it. Today: Nawab Kapur Singh.
screen: `A HOT DAY. A MAN WITH A FAN.` → `AN OFFER FROM LAHORE.` → `WHO WILL WEAR THE TITLE?`

segments.voice: Why would a governor who had hunted the Sikhs offer them a title? Tradition says force had not worked, so he tried another way: give them land and rank, and perhaps they would settle down and stop resisting. The Khalsa met to discuss it. Some did not want any title from the government that had killed their people. Others saw a chance for a little breathing room. And the leaders who were asked to take it, tradition says, turned it down. So the gathering made a remarkable decision. The title would go to the one doing seva. They looked around, and there was Kapur Singh, still fanning the sangat. And that was how the title found its man: not to the loudest, not to the most powerful, but to the one with the fan in his hand. Kapur Singh did not grab it. Tradition says he would accept the robe of honor only after it had been touched to the feet of five respected Sikhs, as if to say the honor belonged to the Khalsa, and he was only carrying it. And he asked one more thing: that being a nawab would never excuse him from his old service. Some tellings say his seva was cleaning the stables and tending the horses, and he kept at it. He went on to become a leader of the whole Khalsa, organizing it in the hard years ahead. But the story keeps the fan in its first scene. Seva means selfless service, and the tradition holds that it is the root that leadership grows from, not a step to climb past.
screen: `A GOVERNOR'S OFFER: LAND AND A TITLE.` · `THE LEADERS TURN IT DOWN.` · `GIVE IT TO THE ONE DOING SEVA.` · `TOUCHED TO THE FEET OF FIVE SIKHS.` · then, large: `THE HUMBLE NAWAB.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fan someone in the heat. Sit, and let the breath cool and slow. Then bring to mind one person in your life who is under pressure right now. Tired, stretched, overheated in some way. What would a fan look like for them? A glass of water brought without asking. A chore taken off their list. Ten quiet minutes so they can rest. Picture yourself doing it, without needing them to notice. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Nawab Kapur Singh. The Sikh who was fanning the sangat when the Khalsa chose him for a governor's title, and who took it only on condition he could keep serving. Today's word.

Your line: the humble nawab. Today, bring one cooling thing to someone under pressure, a glass of water or a chore off their list, then go back to your own work without waiting to be noticed. Day eight hundred fifty-two.

853.title: The two Dals
853.hook: the Khalsa organized into the elders' army and the young army
853.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Budha Dal and Taruna Dal as the Khalsa's organization under Nawab Kapur Singh, and Nihang Sikh groups today still carry the name Budha Dal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nawab Kapur Singh, the man with the fan who was given a governor's title. Your line was the humble nawab. Who did you cool down? Today, what the humble nawab built. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

Here is a tension that turns up in families, in teams, in congregations. The young want to move. The old want to keep. The young say: you're too careful. The old say: you're too quick. Sometimes one side wins and the other drifts away. The Khalsa, in its hard century, had both kinds of Sikh in its ranks, with real lives at stake. And tradition says that under Nawab Kapur Singh each was given a name and a job. Today: the two Dals.
screen: `THE YOUNG WANT TO MOVE.` → `THE OLD WANT TO KEEP.` → `A NAME AND A JOB FOR EACH.`

segments.voice: Dal means a host, an army, a body of people moving together. Tradition says that under Nawab Kapur Singh the Khalsa was organized into two of them. The Budha Dal, the army of the elders. And the Taruna Dal, the army of the young. Each had its own work. The tellings say the Budha Dal, the older Sikhs, looked after the holy places and the steady life of the community, and gave counsel. The Taruna Dal, the younger riders, took on the fast, dangerous work of defense, moving where they were needed. Neither was the junior partner. The elders were not pushed aside as too slow. The young were not held back as too reckless. In the tellings, they were separate, but not apart. Tradition says that when the Khalsa gathered at Amritsar, both Dals came together, sat in the same sangat, and made decisions as one. The young had the elders' memory. The elders had the young's strength. And over both stood a shared allegiance: not to a Dal, but to the Guru's way. Tradition says the Taruna Dal later grew and was divided into smaller bands, and those bands, in time, became the seeds of something bigger. But today the point is simpler. A community needs its grandparents and its teenagers. It needs the ones who remember why and the ones who can still run. The two Dals are a picture of how not to waste either.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect both elders and youth. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind one person in your life who is a good deal older than you. Let one thing they know, that you don't, come to mind. Then bring to mind one person a good deal younger. Let one thing they can do, that you can't anymore, or never could, come to mind. Hold the two of them side by side for a while. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The two Dals. The Budha Dal of the elders and the Taruna Dal of the young, two bodies of the Khalsa with different work and one shared sangat. Today's word.
Your line: old and young together. Today, ask one older person for their advice, and ask one younger person to show you something. Day eight hundred fifty-three.

854.title: Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh
854.hook: two Sikhs rode into Amritsar in disguise to end a desecration of the Harmandir in 1740
854.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh as a defense of the Harmandir's sanctity, and it is often recalled in gurdwara talks about the Khalsa's hard century.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the two Dals, elders and young in one sangat. Your line was old and young together. This week: Mata Sundari's letters, the forests, a toll on the highway, the Diwali permit, a nawab with a fan, and the two Dals. Day eight hundred fifty-four.

Far to the south, in the dry country where hunted Sikhs had taken refuge, a traveler from Amritsar arrives with news nobody wants to hear. The Harmandir, the house of the Guru at the center of the sacred pool, has been taken over by a local official. Tradition says he is using it for drinking parties and dancing, inside the place where the Guru's hymns are sung. The listeners are silent. Then two men stand up. Today: Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh.
screen: `NEWS FROM AMRITSAR.` → `THE HARMANDIR DESECRATED.` → `TWO MEN STAND UP.`

segments.voice: The official was named Massa Ranghar, and in the tradition he becomes a picture of contempt: someone who took a holy place and filled it with exactly what it was not for. Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh decided to end it. But they could not march an army into Amritsar. So they used a disguise. Tradition says they dressed as village headmen coming to pay revenue, and filled their bags with something that clinked like coins. Some tellings say broken pieces of pottery, cut round. They rode into Amritsar, tied their horses outside, and walked in carrying their bags as if they had come to pay what was owed. They were let through. Inside, they found Massa Ranghar at his entertainment. Tradition says they struck him down, and were back on their horses and gone before the guards understood what had happened. The story is told with fire, and it's worth saying what the tradition sees in it. Not a love of violence. The Harmandir belongs to the Guru and to everyone who comes to it; its doors, Sikhs say, open in every direction. Using it for mockery was an attack on what it stands for. The two riders were not after loot or power. They rode in to give the place back to its purpose. A hard story, honestly told. But the image that stays is the two horses outside the gate, and two men who had every reason to stay safe in the desert, choosing not to.
screen: `THE HARMANDIR TAKEN OVER.` · `DISGUISED AS MEN PAYING REVENUE.` · `IN AND GONE BEFORE THE GUARDS KNEW.` · `NOT LOOT. THE PLACE'S PURPOSE.` · then, large: `THEY RODE IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: defend something sacred. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one thing that is sacred to you, or simply precious. A place. A practice. A person's dignity. A quiet hour you protect. Then notice where it's being crowded or mocked, even a little, even by your own habits. What would it take to give it back its purpose? Let one small, peaceful step come to mind. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Mehtab Singh and Sukha Singh. The two Sikhs who, tradition says, rode into Amritsar in disguise to end Massa Ranghar's desecration of the Harmandir. Today's word.
screen: `MEHTAB SINGH AND SUKHA SINGH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: they rode in. Today, take one peaceful step to protect something sacred to you from whatever has been crowding it. Day eight hundred fifty-four.

fork.setup: you're Mehtab Singh, safe in the desert. news comes that the Harmandir is being used for drinking and dancing. you can't bring an army. what do you do?
options: stay safe and pray it ends.
ride in disguise, as men paying revenue, and end it yourselves.
write a complaint to the governor.
fork.reveal: tradition says he and Sukha Singh rode in disguised as headmen with bags of false coins, struck down Massa Ranghar, and escaped.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Harmandir Sahib, the house of the Guru at Amritsar.

trapdoor: what you thought: a revenge story.
what it means: two Sikhs risked everything to end the mockery of the Harmandir and give it back its purpose.
what a scholar hears: a tradition recorded in Rattan Singh Bhangu's Panth Prakash, set in the governorship of Zakariya Khan.
